_readme: Principal spatial templates extracted from real museum floor plans (multi-agent extraction 2026-07-21, 8 museums, 8/8 agents clean). Each template abstracts the museum's principal idea into the /template-maps cell vocabulary; tiles are merged into template_patterns.json (mode stamp) for the editor and map making. Provenance: literature+abstraction — templates PROPOSE (P-10); numbers carry their sources. Validation: dims/tokens/top-to-bottom walkability/stop pockets, results per entry. WAVE 5 (2026-08-05): eight NON-museum buildings that stage a walk past things — the gene pool was entirely art museums, which all assume plinth, distance and a hero; these argue otherwise (each carries not_a_museum).
extracted: 2026-07-21 (8 museums) + 2026-07-31 (6 more, multi-agent; legacy tiles repaired for the collision walker; gate = tools/validate_museum_templates.py) + 2026-08-02 wave 3 (Pompidou/Teshima/Mezquita extracted, first edited-lineage tiles as challengers)

museums.architect: Giorgio Vasari, 1560-1581 (completed by Buontalenti and Parigi; Tribuna by Buontalenti, 1584)
museums.circulation_type: enfilade off a U-shaped spine corridor (single-loaded statue-lined corridor with lateral room enfilade)
museums.mechanism: The U-corridor separates flow from seeing: movement, daylight, and the long end-stopped vista belong to the statue-lined spine, while stationary looking is decanted into optional enfilade rooms one door off the spine, so stopping to see never blocks the walk.

museums.walk_rule: Enter at the head of the east spine and walk the 3-wide corridor pulled forward by the hero visible on-axis 27 cells ahead, dipping optionally through door gaps into three side rooms whose aligned doors form a second parallel vista, then turn west along the south corridor past the hero and exit on the enfilade axis.
museums.pacing_rule: Paired podium statues line the spine's inner wall in bays broken by door gaps (Vasari's three-bays-plus-narrow-bay rhythm), and every pause option sits off the clear lane so lingering never dams the flow; the one mandated stop is the raised dais step before the end-stopped hero.

museums.museum: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York
museums.architect: Frank Lloyd Wright, 1959
museums.circulation_type: forced single path (continuous spiral ramp; abstracted as switchback serpentine)
museums.mechanism: By collapsing all circulation into one gently sloped descending ramp, the plan removes route choice entirely — flow is automatic — while shallow web-wall bays create stop pockets just off the moving path and the open central void lets visitors preview and re-encounter works across the atrium before and after passing them.

museums.walk_rule: Enter at the top (the elevator drop-off) and walk one un-branching serpentine: each 3-wide lane runs the full width, turns through a 3-cell gap at the alternating end of each partition, and empties onto the rotunda floor at the bottom where the hero stands on the atrium axis.
museums.pacing_rule: Movement never pauses the route — art bays are recessed into the solid partition stretches as stop pockets beside the flow, while the aligned see-through void windows (c6-c8) form the atrium axis that promises the hero podium from up to 27 cells away and re-shows passed works across lanes.

museums.architect: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, 1968
museums.circulation_type: free-plan matrix
museums.mechanism: By clearing the entire 50 m span of structure and putting art on freestanding walls and suspended panels, the plan makes flow and seeing the same act — the visitor self-routes through a matrix of view-objects, and no wall ever hides the next work for long.

museums.walk_rule: Enter anywhere on the open top edge and drift freely through a column-free field; freestanding picture-walls and podia are obstacles to orbit, not corridors to follow, and the only fixed event is the on-axis hero at the hall's centre.
museums.pacing_rule: Pacing comes from paired off-axis freestanding walls at each third of the walk that slow the drift into eddies, while the untouched central axis keeps a 13-cell promise to the hero so the visitor always chooses between lingering and advancing.

museums.museum: Sir John Soane's Museum, 13 Lincoln's Inn Fields, London
museums.architect: Sir John Soane, 1792-1824 (house rebuilt in three campaigns; museum arranged until his death 1837)
museums.circulation_type: cabinet — a dense wunderkammer loop of tiny interconnected rooms threaded on narrow passages, with one end-stopped axial vista to the deepest point
museums.mechanism: Soane resolves flow versus seeing by making every wall of the narrow path itself the display and letting the eye outrun the body — layered apertures (colonnade screens, floor cuts to the crypt, folding picture-planes) show objects several rooms ahead, so walking is compressed to a shuffle while seeing is multiplied in depth.

museums.walk_rule: A 3-wide spine runs the full axis while staggered door gaps pull the body sideways into small 3x4 cabinet pockets; the eye keeps the long axial vista to the hero as the feet loop room by room.
museums.pacing_rule: Every five rows a cross-wall with corridor-facing niche slots compresses the walk back onto the spine, alternating pocket-dwell and corridor-glide, until the terminal dome room releases the width and the hero end-stops the 16-cell sightline just before a blind wall.

museums.architect: Carlo Scarpa, 1959-1973
museums.circulation_type: forced single path: end-stopped enfilade with off-axis display (loop at building scale)
museums.mechanism: Aligned door openings fuse five rooms into one long axial vista that promises the terminus (flow), while every sculpture is displaced off that axis with its own facing direction — a network of gazes that pulls the walker sideways into stops — and the axis itself is end-stopped at the Cangrande hinge, where a single hero on a raised plinth owns a whole bay and is circled rather than passed.

museums.walk_rule: Enter on the central axis and cross four rooms through aligned 3-wide door gaps; in each room the works sit off-axis so you drift sideways to a stop pocket and return to the line, until the axis delivers you into the hero bay where you circle the raised podium and exit through the off-axis side door behind it.
museums.pacing_rule: The hero is visible from the entrance through every aligned gap (a 24-cell promise), but four cross walls each impose a pause-and-drift beat before the axis is allowed to resolve, and the end-stop wall plus sideways exit ensure the vista terminates on the hero instead of continuing past it.

museums.architect: Louis Métezeau & Jacques II Androuet du Cerceau, 1595–1607 (bay rhythm: Percier & Fontaine, 1805–1810; skylights: Lefuel, 1860s)
museums.circulation_type: forced single path — continuous axial promenade with walk-past wall hang, rhythmed by bays
museums.mechanism: A single very long, 13 m-wide axis keeps everyone flowing toward an endless vanishing point, while nine column-framed bays with overhead skylights pinch the walk into regular stopping pockets where the continuous wall hang can be faced one painting at a time.

museums.walk_rule: Enter on axis and drift down the wide central lane toward the hero visible from the first step; at each bay, step sideways into the wall pocket to face a slot, then rejoin the flow, finally rounding the end-stopped hero to exit.
museums.pacing_rule: Paired column cells pinch the 13-cell width every 4 rows into nine bays, and each bay's midpoint row carries a facing pair of wall slots — a metronome of stop-beats under one uninterrupted 33-cell sightline.

museums.museum: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa
museums.architect: SANAA (Kazuyo Sejima + Ryue Nishizawa), 2004
museums.circulation_type: free-plan matrix — independent room-boxes floating in a multi-entry, non-hierarchical circulation field
museums.mechanism: Flow and seeing never compete because they occupy different spaces: movement is free in the daylight corridor-streets between boxes, while each artwork gets a sealed room individually tuned (size 18–324 m², height 4–12 m, light) to seeing it, entered and exited at the visitor's choice.

museums.walk_rule: Enter anywhere along the open top edge; parallel streets (west 3-wide, central 3-wide, east lane) and full-width cross streets loop around sealed room-boxes, and the central street's promised hero room dead-ends, sending the walker back into the field to choose an exit route.
museums.pacing_rule: Seeing is quantized into rooms — pace is the number of boxes you elect to enter and leave through the street field, not distance walked; corridor-hung slots give the streets themselves exhibition weight between stops.

museums.architect: Robert Venturi & Denise Scott Brown (VSBA, with Sheppard Robson), 1991
museums.circulation_type: enfilade — three parallel lines of galleries off a skewed axis; the central line is a true on-axis enfilade with false-perspective diminishing arches, the side lines have offset doorways that deliberately interrupt the vistas
museums.mechanism: The central nave-like enfilade makes one long promise — Cima's altarpiece glimpsed through five diminishing arches at the deepest point pulls flow forward — while the flanking rooms, entered through offset doors that break the lateral sightlines, decompress into small domestic-scale chambers where stopping and seeing individual panels is the default.

museums.walk_rule: Enter on-axis at the top and the hero is already visible 28 cells away through every door gap; the 3-wide central nave carries the flow straight to the raised hero chamber, while offset side doors peel viewers into 3-cell-wide cabinet rooms and return them to the axis one bay deeper.
museums.pacing_rule: Cross walls every 5-6 rows frame the vista and the door gaps narrow as you go (5, 5, 3, 3 cells) — a false perspective that makes the hero feel farther then suddenly near — with the final threshold stepping up onto a platform where the 3s altarpiece slot is end-stopped by the terminal wall and the exit turns off-axis, exactly as the wing hands you sideways to the bridge.

museums.architect: Karl Friedrich Schinkel (designed 1822/23, built 1825-1830)
museums.circulation_type: central rotunda hub with wrapping perimeter galleries
museums.mechanism: A Pantheon-derived rotunda sits at the dead center of a symmetrical rectangle, and everything else — vestibule, stair hall, wing galleries — is reached from it and returns to it. The rotunda resolves flow vs seeing by separating them in time: the wings are for walking and looking along walls, the rotunda is for stopping, recalibrating, and choosing the next wing. Arrival is a rite of passage down the axis; orientation is never lost because the hub is always one door away.

museums.walk_rule: The walker enters at the top gap onto the x=7 axis, crosses the vestibule and the screen-wall door at row 5, passes the stair-hall antechamber into the rotunda's north door at row 10, and from the rotunda's four doors (rows 10/18 at x=7, row 14 at x=4/x=10) makes out-and-back loops into the flanking wing corridors before leaving by the south door and the bottom gap.
museums.pacing_rule: Stopping concentrates inside the rotunda ring (the hero at 14,7 and the four 1s statue niches against the chamfered corners) and at the 2s podiums pressed against the wing outer walls, while the x=7 spine and the row-14 cross-axis stay entirely slot-free, so a pausing viewer never blocks the through-path.

museums.architect: Frank Gehry (1997)
museums.circulation_type: atrium radial
museums.mechanism: A 45 m light-filled atrium is the fixed center of gravity: galleries do not chain into each other, they radiate off the atrium, and the visitor returns to the lit center after every room, so orientation is never lost and each gallery is a fresh departure rather than a link in a corridor. Flow and seeing are resolved by separation of duties — the atrium carries all movement while the pockets hold all looking — and one exceptional elongated gallery (the 130 m boat gallery) breaks the radial rhythm to give a single oversized work a space scaled to it alone.

museums.walk_rule: Enter the top gap into the lobby, pass the center door into the 5-cell-wide atrium shaft and ride it south, stepping through single-cell side doors (rows 6/11/16 left, 7/12/17 right) into 3x4 gallery pockets and back to the shaft each time, then take the narrow row-19 door into the 13-cell-wide boat gallery, weave among its podiums past the central hero, and leave through the terrace to the bottom gap.
museums.pacing_rule: All stopping happens one door off the spine — inside the six radiating pockets and around the flanked hero in the long gallery — while the atrium shaft itself holds no slots, so the lit center always carries through-flow and every pause is a fresh departure that never dams the walk.

museums.architect: Tadao Ando
museums.circulation_type: buried single-file descent — dark 1-wide corridors linking isolated one-work cells
museums.mechanism: THE BURIED CELL: the museum is sunk into the hilltop so that almost everything is wall and passage, and each of its very few works occupies its own sealed room. Long, deliberately dark and narrow approach corridors decompress the eye between rooms, so arrival in each lit chamber lands as an event. The passage is the frame; the collection is barely a handful of works by exactly three artists.

museums.architect: OpenOffice (Alan Koch, Lyn Rice, Galia Solomonoff, Linda Taalman) with artist Robert Irwin, 2003 — conversion of a 1929 Nabisco box-printing factory
museums.circulation_type: field of bays — free drift across a single-story daylight shed on a column grid, no prescribed route
museums.mechanism: A vast one-level factory floor is kept as one continuous space under sawtooth skylights, structured only by the regular rhythm of freestanding columns. Each column-bounded bay is given whole to a single artist, so scale itself becomes the curator: you drift laterally between parallel bays rather than following a sequence. Partial divider stubs mark where one artist ends and another begins without ever closing a room.

museums.architect: Daniel Libeskind
museums.circulation_type: zigzag switchback crossed by a straight sealed void axis
museums.mechanism: Libeskind's 'Between the Lines' plan is two lines: a tortuous zigzag you walk and a straight line you cannot enter. Where they intersect, sealed concrete voids cut through every floor — unlit, unheated shafts the visitor keeps colliding with but can never occupy. The walk is organized by what it is denied: circulation bends around absence, and the absence is the exhibit.

museums.walk_rule: Walk the switchbacks: each full-width wall forces a hard turn, the three sealed void chambers on the central columns are never enterable — pass them along their flanking corridors, let the dead-end pockets beside each void deliver you to a slot facing blank wall, and cross the void line only at the open turn rows.

museums.museum: Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk
museums.architect: Jørgen Bo & Vilhelm Wohlert (with Claus Wohlert from the East Wing), 1958–1998
museums.circulation_type: pavilion chain — discrete gallery pavilions strung on a landscape walk, joined by narrow glass links
museums.mechanism: Louisiana is not one building but a chain: discrete whitewashed gallery pavilions set into a coastal park, joined by narrow glazed corridors so that the walk between rooms is itself part of the museum. Each glass link empties the eye onto landscape before the next room begins, so every pavilion is entered fresh, and the 1991 underground Graphics Wing finally closed the chain into a ring. The hero moment is earned at the end of the walk — the Giacometti gallery opening onto the lake.

museums.architect: Abd al-Rahman I (786) through al-Hakam II (961-976) and al-Mansur (987-988); cathedral crossing inserted from 1523 under Bishop Alonso Manrique
museums.circulation_type: isotropic hypostyle field — drift, no axis, no far wall
museums.mechanism: Hypostyle forest: 78 single free-standing columns on a strict every-2nd-cell grid fill the entire interior, so the columns ARE the experience — every aisle repeats every other aisle, orientation dissolves, and unlike Dia:Beacon's rhythm (columns organizing bays) density here is total. The one exception, the mihrab hero plinth, sits off-axis in the southeast of the field, discoverable only by drift; the twelve slots are embedded in the column grid like side chapels, breaking the beat without breaking the field.
numbers: ~850 columns stand today, of jasper, onyx, marble, granite and porphyry — Wikipedia (about 120 in Abd al-Rahman I's original 786 hall)

~1,250-1,300 columns at the mosque's maximum extent before the 16th-century cathedral crossing demolished part of the forest; the commonly cited surviving figure is 856 — Flickr/Socks Studio counts vs. Wikipedia's ~850
Footprint 180 x 130 m (590 x 425 ft) after all expansions — Wikipedia

19 aisles perpendicular to the qibla wall after al-Mansur's 987-988 lateral (eastward-only, river-blocked) expansion, up from the original 11 — Wikipedia; this eastward widening is why the mihrab is off the building's central axis
Mihrab of al-Hakam II completed 971, with Byzantine-influenced gold mosaics finished late 970/early 971 — Wikipedia
Two-tier arches throughout: lower horseshoe + upper semicircular, voussoirs alternating red brick and white stone — Wikipedia / Socks Studio
museums.walk_rule: Enter and lose the door: every aisle repeats every other aisle, so walk by drift, not axis — pick any corridor, turn when a slot breaks the column rhythm, and let the off-axis hero (the mihrab) find you deep in the southeast of the field; the exit is just another gap in the wall, met the same way.
museums.pacing_rule: Metronomic: a column every second cell sets a constant beat with no crescendo and no vista; slots are rests scattered off-symmetry within the beat, the single hero is one held note — density never varies, so all pacing comes from the walker's own turns.

museums.architect: Renzo Piano & Richard Rogers (with Gianfranco Franchini; structure Peter Rice/Arup, gerberettes), 1977
museums.circulation_type: free-plan plateau — one uninterrupted loft floor, all circulation and servicing thrown to the perimeter; visitors drift freely across an open field with the hero at the integration core
museums.mechanism: PLATEAU LIBRE with an INTEGRATED hero. Everything that would interrupt the floor — structure, ducts, stairs, lifts, corridors — is exiled to the long edges as segmented servicing bays hugging the walls (the gerberette zone), leaving the interior a single column-free plateau. The one hero plinth is planted at the exact centre of the plan on the entry-exit axis: the point of maximum visual integration, seen straight down the spine from the entry gap, from the exit gap, and from ~87% of all floor cells (Hillier: occupancy follows visibility — the opposite pole from the Sainsbury's buried hero). Secondary slots sit on freestanding low podiums scattered in the free field, spine kept clear, never walling the hero off.
numbers: 48 m clear structural span per floor — no interior columns, achieved by 48-metre trusses on 800 mm spun-steel hollow columns (RSHP/Archeetect)
~7,500 m2 per free-plan floor plateau, arrangeable for any activity (Archeetect/Metalocus)
166 m x 60 m plan, 103,305 m2 total floor area over 7 above-ground levels — the 13x36 tile matches the 2.77:1 plan ratio (Wikipedia)

16,000 tons of steel with six 10-tonne cast-steel gerberettes per column carrying the perimeter servicing zone, thirteen structural bays — echoed as the segmented '2' bays along the tile's long walls (RSHP)
~50,000 m2 — half the site — surrendered to the public piazza, forcing the servicing to the building edge and the floors to total openness (RSHP)
museums.walk_rule: Enter onto the open plateau and see the hero immediately, dead ahead down the clear central spine. Walk the free field in any order — servicing bays wall the edges, podium slots drift past on both flanks — but every path bends toward the centre, where the hero stands fully in the round before the spine releases you to the exit.
museums.pacing_rule: No enforced sequence: pacing is self-set on one open floor. The hero is met early by eye and late by body — visible from the threshold, reached mid-walk, re-seen from behind on the way out. Slot podiums alternate left-right at even intervals like structural bays, giving a loose rhythm without ever interrupting the plateau.

museums.architect: Ryue Nishizawa (with artist Rei Naito), 2010
museums.circulation_type: single-thread approach into one continuous chamber
museums.mechanism: THE DROPLET — a long winding outdoor approach empties the visitor, then one continuous pillar-free concrete shell holds a single artwork that is the building itself; the museum reduced to a single held breath, the extreme end of the reduction axis (Chichu compresses to five works, Teshima to one)

oval oculi in the shell — no doors or windows; light, wind, rain and sound enter freely (Benesse Art Site)
artworks in the entire museum: Rei Naito's 'Matrix', water rising from the floor — the building and the work are one (Wikipedia / Benesse)

museums.walk_rule: one path only: enter at the gap, serpentine the long outdoor approach for over half the tile's length, pass through the narrow neck into the droplet chamber, circle the single work, leave by the far gap
museums.pacing_rule: the approach is the decompression — no slots, no incident, just walking; then everything at once in one chamber and nothing after; slot density is the lowest in the corpus by design

museums.museum: Capuchin Crypt, Santa Maria della Concezione dei Cappuccini, Via Veneto, Rome
museums.architect: Capuchin friars under Cardinal Antonio Barberini; bones transferred from Via dei Lucchesi 1631, arrangements largely mid-18th century, accumulating burials 1500–1870
museums.circulation_type: Single-aisle one-way lateral procession: an unbranching corridor past six rooms that open onto it but are not entered
museums.mechanism: Flow and seeing are separated by a lip rather than a room: the walker is confined to a two-cell corridor while the collection occupies a raised mass four times its width, so every specimen is seen frontally, at a fixed unclosable distance, embedded in a continuous surface rather than standing free.
museums.not_a_museum: A museum gallery is a room you enter to be among the objects; here the only room you are permitted to enter is the one that contains no remains, and it holds the only object that stands on your own floor — so the building stages refusal of approach as its entire content, which no plinth-and-aisle gallery can do.
museums.walk_rule: One two-cell corridor runs the full length of the tile. No branch, no loop, no return, no choice — the body enters at the top and leaves at the bottom having walked a tube. Every bone chapel opens to the right as a raised mass the walker can only look into: the '2' lip at the corridor edge is the barrier, and each slot sits one step beyond it, so the reach is always one cell short. The walker's floor is 60 of 390 cells; the collection's volume is four times larger and entirely off-limits. Exactly one threshold opens — the walkable side-room at rows 7-10 — and it is the only room in the tile whose object is a floor slot standing on the walker's own floor, with no lip and no podium between.
museums.pacing_rule: Six openings in thirty rows, each sealed off from the next by a one-row wall pier, so the corridor closes and reopens six times. The framing rooms (rows 2-5, rows 24-27) are four rows deep; the three taxonomic chapels between them are three rows each — a fast even drumbeat of one-bone-type-per-room, skulls then pelvises then femurs. Chapel depth swells backwards as you go (six cells, seven, six, eight, eight) while the corridor never widens by a single cell. The hero is stopped at exactly the same lip as the femur wall: content escalates, access never does.

museums.architect: Commissioned by Septimius Severus / completed under Caracalla, architect unrecorded; built AD 212–216/217, Severan imperial Rome
museums.circulation_type: Mirrored axial enfilade of thermal states — two identical wings flanking one shared central spine, alternating split/merge, terminating in a domed rotunda that blocks the axis and forces a retrograde back through the same rooms in reverse temperature order
museums.mechanism: Flow runs on the axis and seeing runs on the walls: every basin, niche and statue is set into the flanking thickness so the body never has to stop facing forward, while the one thing standing on the axis — the domed hot core — cannot be entered at all, only committed to on one side and orbited at a podium's remove, so approach and vision are held permanently at right angles.
museums.not_a_museum: A bath stages a body that is being changed — heated, scraped, plunged, cooled — so the room itself is the exhibit and the objects are incidental furniture you pass while becoming something else; a gallery can only ever stage a body that stays the same and accumulates looks.
museums.walk_rule: Walk the spine and let it keep changing your number: broad merged halls (portico, frigidarium) put one body on the axis, then the pool and the rotunda split you into two mirrored aisles that cannot see across. At the core you must commit to a side — there is no crossing the centre line — and you re-merge only after passing it. Past the core the tile is its own reflection: the same three bands in reverse order, so the exit walk is the entry walk read backwards at a different temperature.
museums.pacing_rule: Nothing stands on the axis except the one hero, and the hero is unreachable — every other slot is pushed into the flanking wall thickness as a niche, so the body reads sideways while moving forward and never stops to face a thing head-on. Split bands are silent: the natatio and rotunda aisles carry no slots at all, because a body crossing a state should have nothing to look at. Merged bands carry the podia, one pair per hall, always at the outer wall. Dwell should climb through the pinch, spike in the orbit where the hero is passed twice at one podium's remove and touched never, then decay through the mirrored half, where the same rooms are met a second time and should be given roughly half the time — the return is recognition, not discovery.

museums.museum: Katsura Imperial Villa (Katsura Rikyū), Kyoto — the chisen-kaiyū-shiki (pond stroll) garden and its circuit path
museums.architect: Prince Hachijō Toshihito and Prince Toshitada, with the Kobori Enshū circle credited by tradition; built in phases c. 1615–1662 (early Edo)
museums.circulation_type: Forced single-thread serpentine circuit around an uncrossable water body — three descending/ascending legs, baffled sightlines (miegakure), one obligatory turn-chamber at the far apex, and a released return
museums.mechanism: Seeing is rationed by walking: the pond is a hole in the walkable world, so the body must go down one shore, along the beach, and back up the other before it can reach anything, and the corridor is baffled so that every straight run dies against a wall or mound within six cells — you look down at your feet, turn, and only in the turn does anything open.
museums.not_a_museum: A museum gallery lets you see the object from the door and decide whether to approach; here the hero sits seven cells from the entrance in plan and seventy-nine steps away on foot, and the only door between the up-leg and the down-leg is the cell beside it — you cannot browse, skip, or approach frontally, you can only arrive.
museums.walk_rule: One forced thread, no branches. Enter top-centre on a narrow three-cell approach (the Miyukimichi), walk four cells and hit a wall: the Sumiyoshi-pine blocker turns you west along the tile's one long entry traverse. Descend the west shore (cols 1-2) for twenty-three rows against a wall of alternating baffles and mounds — no straight run over five cells, so the head is down and the next turn is never visible. At the bottom the shore terrace (rows 26-27) runs east under the pond; a podium stands in the middle of it, so even the beach must be walked around. Ascend the east shore (cols 10-11), equally baffled. At the top the corridor narrows into a four-cell chamber (row 5) that is the ONLY connection between the up-leg and the down-leg: the hero podium stands in the wall you turn against, and every body that leaves this tile has stood beside it. Then the release — the outbound leg (col 13) is a single-file descent with only three jogs and the tile's longest sightline, twenty-five rows back down to the exit gate at bottom-right. Total walked ≈112 cells for a tile 32 rows tall.
museums.pacing_rule: Content sits on the inbound legs and is never frontal. Podiums go INSIDE the two-wide corridors so the body squeezes past with the head turned (rows 10 and 12); floor stones sit in the path itself (rows 17, 24, 25) and are read looking down. Never place two slots within four rows of each other on the same leg — the baffles, not the objects, set the rhythm, and an object every fourth turn is the correct density. The shore terrace gets exactly one podium, standing in the open where the head finally comes up. The 3s hero is reserved for the turn-chamber and must never be duplicated in spirit: nothing else in the tile may be approachable head-on. The outbound leg carries at most one item — it is the walk home, and its job is to make the tile's length felt rather than filled.

museums.architect: Henri Labrouste, 1838–1850 (opened 1851)
museums.circulation_type: committed twin-nave spine — six parallel aisles that never cross, hemmed by tables, with the collection sealed at the walls and below the floor
museums.mechanism: The walk is separated from the seeing by a solid centre: a body enters off-axis at the stair corner, commits to one of six longitudinal aisles it cannot leave, and moves the whole length hemmed by reading tables with the book-presses two rows outboard behind grilles — the only object it can actually reach is the delivery desk on axis at the far end, where the hidden ground-floor magasin surfaces.
museums.not_a_museum: A museum gallery puts the collection in your path so you approach it; this plan puts the collection behind you, above you and beneath you, and gives you instead a long file of places to SIT — the thing you came for is fetched from a room you never enter, so the tile stages waiting and passage rather than looking.
museums.walk_rule: Enter off-axis at the corner (the stair does not take space from the room), cross a 3-row head band, then COMMIT: the centre spine is solid for 25 rows, so a body picks one of six parallel aisles and cannot change nave until the spine terminates in the delivery desk. Exit is on the centre axis, so every traversal turns from edge to middle and passes the one reachable object last.
museums.pacing_rule: Bay period 5. Table rows break laterally on rows 8/13/18/23 (within a nave only, never across the spine) — that is the arch bay. Wall book-presses fire on rows 6/11/16/21/26, reading-table lamps on rows 5/15/25, so the two slot families alternate on off-beats and a slot passes the shoulder every 2–3 steps. NO floor slots at all: nothing in this building stands in your path, everything is furniture you go around or shelving you cannot reach. The single 3s sits on the spine axis at row 29 — the counter where the hidden stack surfaces.

museums.architect: Giuseppe Mengoni — competition design 1861, built 1865–1877 (Mengoni died in a fall from the scaffolding days before the 1878 inauguration)
museums.circulation_type: Thoroughfare — a glazed public street, cruciform in plan, open at both ends of the long arm onto two city squares, with an octagonal rotunda at the crossing; no terminus, no route, no ticket
museums.mechanism: Flow is never interrupted for seeing: the goods sit behind a continuous glazed band at the walker's shoulder, so attention is paid at walking speed and in the periphery, and the plan's single concession to stopping is the octagonal crossing, where the band steps back, four ways meet, and an intersection becomes a room you can stand still in.
museums.not_a_museum: It is a public street with two open ends and a destination beyond itself, so the walk owes nothing to what is displayed — no one can be made to finish it, and the display has to earn a turned head from a body already going somewhere else.
museums.walk_rule: The walker is passing through, not visiting. Both ends are portals onto somewhere else, so there is no terminus and no reward for completion; the walkable channel runs unbroken from row 0 to row 32 and the body never has to turn around. Display is lateral and continuous — a raised glazed band pressed against both walls at the shoulder, approached obliquely at walking speed, never frontally. Nothing in the arms can be circled or stood in front of squarely. The one exception is the octagon at mid-tile, where the band steps back to the chamfered faces, the room widens to the full frame, two lateral arms open and immediately meet their own end walls, and the single hero object sits dead centre in the walking line so the walk must part around it. That detour is the only stop the plan asks for.
museums.pacing_rule: In the arms: one wall slot every two rows, alternating left and right (rows 1,5,9 left / 3,7 right, mirrored south), with plain raised band filling every row in between — the band is never empty, so the walker registers merchandise as a texture and the slots as a beat. The head swings, the feet do not stop. Nothing sits in the middle of the street. At the crossing the beat breaks: four chamfer podiums at the diagonal corners (rows 12 and 20), two exedra podiums at the dead ends of the lateral arms (row 16, both frame edges) — the only slots in the tile a body can walk straight at — four floor medallions quartering the rotunda floor (rows 14 and 18), and one hero at centre with walkable cells on all four sides. Ratio matters: twenty-two slots you slide past, three you can face, one you can orbit.

museums.museum: Panorama Mesdag, Zeestraat 65, The Hague — purpose-built panorama rotunda housing the Panorama van Scheveningen (1881), the oldest panorama in the world still on its original site
museums.architect: Gerardus Klomp (1834–1882) designed and developed the rotunda, 1880–81, for the Belgian Société Anonyme des Panoramas; the faux terrain (artificial dune) inside was designed by architect Cornelis Johan Laarman (1844–1889); the Zeestraat entrance building and garden between street and drum reworked 1910–11 under Mesdag. Opened 1 August 1881.
museums.circulation_type: Single-station rotunda: a dark, slotless approach corridor, a stair, one radial trench through the artificial dune, one fixed central viewing platform, and a second trench out — the visitor stops walking and rotates instead. The work is the enclosing wall and is separated from the body by an uncrossable raised terrain at every point of the circle.
museums.mechanism: The plan converts locomotion into rotation: all walkable ground is compressed into a narrow blind approach and a 3×3 platform, while the entire seeing-surface is pushed to a fixed radius behind a continuous band of raised faux terrain, so the only way to change the view is to turn on the spot — distance to the work is a constant the body cannot alter.
museums.not_a_museum: A gallery rewards walking with more and closer looking; this building removes approach as an option entirely — the largest thing in it is met from one immovable foot position, at one distance, forever, which is a spatial argument no room full of approachable objects can make.
museums.walk_rule: Enter narrow and blind. The approach is two cells wide, dog-legs once, compresses to one cell, and carries ZERO slots for eight rows — there is deliberately nothing to see while walking. It pierces the drum wall as a one-cell trench with raised dune on both sides, so the chamber is invisible until the last step. The body emerges onto the 3×3 platform at its north-west corner and must cross to the south-east corner to find the descent: the only motion the platform grants is a turn. Everything else inside the drum is raised terrain — the hero is two cells from the feet, with one band of sand between, and cannot be reached from any cell in the tile. Exactly one small slot (the 1s on the platform) is touchable; the enormous one never is.
museums.pacing_rule: This is a terminal beat, not a sequence. Give the tunnels no camera stations and no dwell at all — they are pure duration. Give the platform 3–4× a normal gallery stop and let the sightline sweep a full 360° from a fixed foot position; the hero sits on the axis opposite the entry trench so it is first met by turning, never by approaching. Do not chain two of these back to back and do not splice a drum into a fast run — put at least one ordinary walked tile on each side, or the darkness reads as loading rather than as preparation.

museums.museum: Sandō (processional approach): Senbon Torii at Fushimi Inari Taisha, Kyoto — read together with the Naikū sandō at Ise Jingū, Mie
museums.architect: Anonymous and accreted. Fushimi Inari founded 711 CE; the torii tunnels are donated gates accumulated from the Edo period (1600s) onward and continuously replaced by Hasegawa Kōmuten. Ise Jingū's sandō, Uji Bridge and torii are rebuilt from scratch every 20 years under Shikinen Sengū (since 690 CE).
museums.circulation_type: Single-file processional threshold run — a repeated pinch-and-release rhythm of gates, with a two-lane fork whose branches are interchangeable, ending at a screened terminus the path passes beside rather than arrives at
museums.mechanism: Flow and seeing are collapsed into one act: the corridor is squeezed to a single cell at every gate so the only thing a body can look at is the frame it is currently passing through, and the one object that would reward stopping is set behind a screen where it can be seen but never reached.
museums.not_a_museum: A gallery gives you objects to halt in front of; this plan gives you a cadence that only exists while you keep moving and then withholds its hero entirely — the content is the interval between thresholds, which no hang of works on a wall can produce.
museums.walk_rule: Single file, always. The corridor pinches to one cell at every gate row and there is no bay wide enough to step aside in; a body behind you cannot pass. At row 9 the path splits into two identical one-cell lanes with a solid spine between them — commit to one, you cannot cross back until row 21. The hero at row 29 is passed on the right shoulder behind a screen and is never faced; the walk continues straight out the bottom without turning to it.
museums.pacing_rule: The sixteen 1s throats are ONE artifact instanced sixteen times, never sixteen different works — vary only scale and hue along the run (small and tight at rows 2–8, widest and heaviest at rows 23–27). Both fork lanes carry the same five instances so the choice is genuinely empty. The three 2s are the only stoppable objects and are votive duplicates of each other, deliberately unremarkable. The single 3s gets its stop pocket only through the 2s screen at row 29: it must be lit and legible from row 29 col 6 and physically unreachable from anywhere.

museums.museum: Le Thoronet Abbey cloister, Provence (Var), France
museums.architect: Anonymous Cistercian master masons of the Order; abbey 1160–1190, cloister galleries begun c. 1175 and completed early 13th century
museums.circulation_type: Closed circumambulation around an impassable void — peripheral-only movement, bidirectional, no chord across the centre; the arcade is a 1.5 m-thick pierced wall that lets the centre be seen but never entered
museums.mechanism: The garth is literally impassable, so the tile offers no chord: to advance twenty-eight rows you walk seventy-odd cells around the outside of a square you may never enter, while the arcade meters that void into pier–bay–pier–bay so the centre arrives only in slices, and a rock outcrop from the hillside pinches the west walk to single file where the ground drops.
museums.not_a_museum: A gallery guarantees you the whole collection along one route, but the ring gives you a choice of direction and hides the other half — the single hero, the hexagonal lavabo, sits on one arm only, so half of all walkers never meet it, and the thing at the centre of the composition is nothing at all.
museums.walk_rule: Enter by the north-east door and leave by the south-west; the centre is void so no step may cross it, and the two mirror-equal arms of the ring (north-then-west, or east-then-south) both reach the exit. The direction chosen decides which half of the contents is never met — the lavabo hero sits on the north arm alone. All four galleries stay continuous, as in the building; nothing is walled off to force the detour, the emptiness in the middle does all the forcing.
museums.pacing_rule: Along the whole inner edge the arcade alternates pier (4) and bay (2) without pause — solid, opening, solid, opening — so the garth is metered rather than given whole; a slot sits in roughly every third bay, and the podium slots face the void so what stands in the opening is read against nothing. The floor stays almost bare: six floor slots across seventy-six cells of gallery, Cistercian sparsity as a rate, not a mood. One pinch at rows 15–16 (the hillside rock at the seven-step level change) narrows the west walk to a single cell, the only place the body cannot pass two abreast.

numbers.name: Cloister side (average)
numbers.value: ~30 m, in the shape of an elongated trapezoid, not a square
numbers.source_note: fr.wikipedia + en.wikipedia: 'mesure en moyenne 30 mètres de côté', 'in the shape of an elongated trapezoid' following the slope down toward the river

numbers.name: Arcade wall thickness
numbers.value: 1.5 m, pierced with twin round-arched bays on a thick central column, oculus above
numbers.source_note: fr.wikipedia: 'baies géminées percées dans un mur d'un mètre cinquante d'épaisseur'

numbers.name: Level change between galleries
numbers.value: seven steps; the south gallery sits lower than the north, hillside rock left as part of the fabric
numbers.source_note: fr.wikipedia: 'sept marches'; en.wikipedia notes rock from the hillside becoming part of the architecture

numbers.name: Lavabo
numbers.value: hexagonal pavilion, five-sided stone dome on six ogives, upper basin 1.35 m diameter, sixteen taps, two doors
numbers.source_note: fr.wikipedia; en.wikipedia places it 'in the cloister in front of what had been the entrance to the refectory'

numbers.name: Galleries
numbers.value: four, barrel-vaulted (east gallery slightly pointed); built 1175 → early 13th c.; church ~40 × 20 m alongside
numbers.source_note: fr.wikipedia + en.wikipedia; south gallery oldest, then east, north, west
